title: Reading a cumulative-frequency graph
stem:
The cumulative-frequency graph summarizes the waiting times of 60 patients. Its straight segments join $(0,0),(5,10),(10,30),(15,50),(20,60)$, where the first coordinate is minutes. Use linear interpolation between class boundaries.

Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the median and both quartiles.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the interquartile range and the proportion who waited at least 10 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Estimate the mean using the four equal-width classes, and explain why the exact mean is unavailable.

steps.text: Read cumulative frequencies 15, 30 and 45; interpolate on the relevant straight segments.
$Q_1=6.25$, median $10$, and $Q_3=13.75$ minutes.
Subtract quartiles and use the complement of the cumulative frequency at 10.
$IQR=7.50$ minutes; proportion $(60-30)/60=0.50$.
Class frequencies are $10,20,20,10$; use midpoints $2.5,7.5,12.5,17.5$.
The individual waiting times within each class are not supplied, so midpoint and interpolation calculations are estimates.

title: A stratified school survey
stem:
A school has 420 junior, 300 middle and 180 senior students. A survey will select 90 students, using proportional stratified random sampling. A previous online poll received responses from 60 junior, 20 middle and 10 senior students.

Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the required sample size in each stratum.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Of the previous poll respondents, 42 junior, 10 middle and 3 senior students supported a proposal. Compare the unweighted respondent support rate with an estimate weighted by the school’s stratum proportions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why weighting the previous poll does not remove all its possible bias.

steps.text: The sampling fraction is $90/900=0.1$.
Junior 42, middle 30, senior 18.
Unweighted rate is $55/90$; weighted rate uses $420/900,300/900,180/900$.
Unweighted $61.1111\%$; weighted $55.3333\%$.
Respondents volunteered rather than being randomly selected within each stratum.
Supporters may be more likely to respond, so within-stratum response bias can remain.

title: Changing the scale of a test score
stem:
A test has mean score 48 and standard deviation 7.5. The exam board converts every score $x$ to $y=1.2x+8$. A score of at least 80 on the converted scale earns a distinction.

Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the converted mean and standard deviation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the minimum original score corresponding to a distinction. Original scores are whole numbers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain whether adding 8 points to every score changes the spread or the number of standard deviations between a score and the mean.

steps.text: The mean transforms by the full affine rule; standard deviation is multiplied only by the positive scale factor.
Mean $65.6$; standard deviation $9$.
Solve $1.2x+8\geq80$.
$x\geq60$, so minimum 60.
Adding a constant shifts all scores and the mean equally, leaving pairwise differences unchanged.
It therefore does not change the standard deviation or standardized relative position.

title: Why reversing a regression is not the same fit
stem:
A sample of trees has diameter $x$ centimetres and height $y$ metres. Technology gives the regression of height on diameter as $y=0.42x+3.6$, and the regression of diameter on height as $x=2.10y-4.8$. Observed diameters range from 10 to 40 cm.

Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Predict the height of a tree of diameter 25 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the diameter of a tree of height 15 m. Compare it with the value obtained by reversing the first regression equation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the two answers differ and which prediction should be used.

steps.text: Use the regression with height as the response variable.
Correct regression: $x=2.10(15)-4.8=26.7$.
Reversing the first line gives $(15-3.6)/0.42=27.1429\ldots$ cm.
The two regressions minimize squared errors in different response variables.
Use 26.7 cm because diameter is being predicted from height; the lines need not be algebraic inverses.

title: Testing a spinner with four equally likely outcomes
stem:
A spinner is claimed to have four equally likely outcomes. It is spun independently 100 times, giving counts 26, 18, 35 and 21. No parameters are estimated from the data. Use a chi-square goodness-of-fit test at 5%.

Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the hypotheses and expected counts.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give a conclusion and explain why the largest count alone is not a complete test of the claim.

steps.text: $H_0$: each outcome has probability 0.25; $H_1$: at least one probability differs.
Multiply 100 by 0.25.
Expected counts $25,25,25,25$.
Use $\sum(O-E)^2/E$ and $df=4-1$.
The p-value exceeds 0.05, so there is insufficient evidence against equally likely outcomes.
The chi-square statistic incorporates deviations in all four categories; a high single count must be assessed relative to the full sampling pattern.

stem:
Two independent random samples complete different training programmes. Their performance scores are shown. Assume the populations are normal with equal variances. Test at 5% whether programme A has the larger population mean.

| Programme A | Programme B |
| --- | --- |
| 18 | 15 |
| 20 | 18 |
| 19 | 17 |
| 21 | 16 |
| 22 | 19 |
| 20 | 17 |



Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Carry out a pooled two-sample t-test using technology. Give the statistic and one-sided p-value.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State the conclusion and explain why treating the rows as matched pairs would be inappropriate.

steps.text: Calculate each mean from the six scores.
The pooled variance is 2; $t=(20-17)/\sqrt{2/6+2/6}$, with $df=10$.
Reject $H_0$ because $p<0.05$; there is evidence that A’s population mean is larger.
The samples are independent and no matching of subjects is described; rows do not create genuine pairs.

title: A p-value at two significance levels
stem:
A pre-planned pooled, unpaired two-sample t-test compares the mean lifetimes of two brands of lamp. The alternative is that the population means differ. Technology reports a two-sided p-value of 0.032. All required sampling and distribution assumptions are satisfied.

Use technology where appropriate. Retain unrounded values until the final answer; give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless money or another precision is specified.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses, and give the decision at the 5% level.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give the decision at the 1% level and explain why the two decisions are consistent.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A report says, “There is a 3.2% probability that the brands have equal mean lifetimes.” Explain the error.

steps.text: $H_0:\mu_A=\mu_B$ and $H_1:\mu_A\ne\mu_B$.
$0.032>0.01$, so do not reject $H_0$ at 1%.
The 1% level demands stronger evidence; a result can meet 5% without meeting 1%.
The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true.
It measures how unusual results at least as extreme would be under that assumption; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
